apply_corrections.prompt_template:
Read `design.md` from the run directory.

The person gave the following corrections when approving the design, or since:

{{gate_corrections}}

Update `design.md` so that every part of it the corrections touch says what they say: the heading (H1), ## Summary, ## Changes and ## Tests, and any optional section the design has (such as ## Rule and sites or ## Docs) whose wording, example text or file list a correction replaces or adds to. Leave no part stating what a correction overrides, because the builder reads the whole document. Keep the sections the corrections do not touch as they are, and keep the document's section headings and structure. Then add a `## Corrections at approval` section, or bring the one the design has up to date: one bullet per correction, quoting it and naming the section(s) of the design that now carry it. Write the updated `design.md`. Return a short message listing what was changed.

audit_corrections.notes: measure each correction's sites in the diff and their tests, as evidence for the overwatch

check.notes: run the brief's check, in a sandbox, beside the reviews

check_design_claims.notes: deterministic check: cited paths exist, quoted lines match within a window, named identifiers are present; resolves drift, lists the rest

classify_reloop.prompt_template:
The person reviewed the design and sent it back with feedback.
Read their feedback above.

Classify whether they want:
- **document**: the feedback is about wording, formatting, structure, missing details, a site, or a test in design.md — the technical approach itself is fine.
- **approach**: the feedback rejects or changes the strategy, architecture, algorithm choice, or component boundaries.

When in doubt, choose approach.

Write exactly one JSON object with two fields:
```json
{"scope": "document" | "approach", "reason": "one-line reason"}
```

classify_scale.notes: classify the change's scale from the research footprint

deliver.notes: push the run's branch and open its pull request, as the approval gate said

delivery_gate.gate_prompt: on authored-file conflict reloop to the builder; otherwise proceed to done

design_doc.prompt_template:
Artifact name: {{name}}
Brief: {{brief}}
It is built in {{source}}.
The check, run from {{check_root}}:
    {{check}}

## The plan
{{strategy}}

{{refine_context}}## Pitfalls
{{pitfalls}}

## What the design checks found
{{design_review_feedback}}


## Strategy gate feedback
{{gate_strategy_feedback}}

{{gate_revision_instruction}}

Acceptance baseline: the original brief, any approved design, and explicit user steering. Preserve user-approved non-goals. A README limitation, proposed exclusion, coordinator summary or reviewer note cannot waive a requested behavior without explicit user agreement to that change. Report conflicts instead of silently narrowing scope. Reviews must mark observed noncompliance as BLOCKING even when the limitation is documented.

Write the design document for this artifact: every file it will add or change, what each one does, the interfaces between them, and how the check exercises them. Be concrete — the next step writes the code from this document and the brief. Specify accepted input syntax and unambiguous rejection behavior: unsupported counts, signs, units, or other values must not silently become different valid requests. For visual output, plan a rendered inspection as well as format/geometry checks, including labels, margins, clipping, and agreement with the requested dimensions.

Make exactly one decision for each design choice — do not present alternatives, do not end a choice with 'a simpler alternative…' or leave it open. A choice left open here becomes an unreviewed decision in the code. Cite every claim about existing code with its file path and line number or range (e.g. `path/to/file.py:42` or `path/to/file.py:42-58`). When claiming what the brief says, quote the brief's words verbatim. The document holds only the final result — no 'Wait—', 'Actually', 'Let me reconsider' or other working-out.

For claims about existing code, use the subject-at-citation-quote form: `name()` at `path/to/file.py:42`: `def name(self):`. The subject (the backtick span before `at`) names the function, attribute or class the claim is about; the quote (the backtick span after `:`) is the line content at that position. This form is mechanically checked, and a claim the check cannot confirm is shown to the person who approves the design. Bare citations without a quoted line (for files being added, or site markers) are fine as-is.

Your design.md must contain, in this order:

1. An H1 heading (`#`) that says what the change does. Never use the run name or artifact name as the title.

2. `## Summary` — the problem and the change, in two to four sentences.

3. `## Changes` — one bullet per file the change adds or modifies: `path` — what changes. This is the one section the build cannot proceed without.

4. `## Tests` — one bullet per test: its repo-relative id (for example `tests/test_foo.py::test_bar`) and what it proves.

When the person corrects the design at the approval gate, the step that applies the corrections adds `## Corrections at approval`; do not write it yourself.

Add any of these optional sections only where it helps the build; leave out the ones that would say nothing:
- `## Failure trace` — for a failure the brief reports, a file:line chain from the symptom to the root cause.
- `## Ask mapping` — a table `| Ask (quoted from brief) | Design section | Test |`, one row per ask, quoting the brief verbatim.
- `## Rule and sites` — the rule the change makes or corrects, then each place in the code that applies or restates it, as a bullet citing file and line, marked [changed] or [left: <reason>].
- `## Test guardedness exemptions` — when a new test passes on the base (for example one that pins existing behaviour), its file path and why it cannot fail without the change. A new test that passes on the base and is not listed here is rejected.
- `## Site revert exemptions` — a changed site that a mechanical revert-and-test cannot catch (logging, a side channel no test observes), as `path:line` and the reason.
- `## Anti-patterns to avoid` — for a high-risk pitfall, the site or § section that handles it, or `[set-aside: <reason>]`.
- `## Docs` — the docs that describe the changed behaviour, and the update each needs.
- `## Core` and `## Behaviour changes` — when the brief asks the pull request for them: the core of the change, and each behaviour a user will see change. Delivery carries both into the pull request's description as written.
- `## Runtime coverage` — which runtimes run the changed code, and how each is covered.

Research and perspective findings — read research/*.md and strategy/*.md directly, and cite a finding id (FND-<slug>-<n>) where it changes a decision. Do not list findings that change nothing; the document is for building the change, not for accounting for the research. The person who approves the design reads it: keep it short.


## Claims check feedback
{{claims_check_feedback}}

emit.prompt_template:
Write the artifact `{{name}}` so that it is complete and runnable.

Brief: {{brief}}
It will be checked by running: {{check}}

## The design
Read the approved design from `design.md` in the run directory.

## What went wrong last time
{{validation}}

## What the reviews refused
{{qa_gate}}
{{overwatch_review}}

Acceptance baseline: the original brief, any approved design, and explicit user steering. Preserve user-approved non-goals. A README limitation, proposed exclusion, coordinator summary or reviewer note cannot waive a requested behavior without explicit user agreement to that change. Report conflicts instead of silently narrowing scope. Reviews must mark observed noncompliance as BLOCKING even when the limitation is documented.

## Your workspace
Your workspace is a prepared clone of the last attempt, with its dependencies installed and its setup and generate commands run; its path is in the execution block above. Make the change there. `git diff HEAD` there shows what you changed since the last attempt; the run's base commit is {{base}}.
Run there, as often as you need, the tests your change touches: the test files you changed or added, and the tests that import the modules you changed. Run the brief's own example or CLI path there too. They run there as they run in the check.
Before you stop, run `refactory-targeted-tests` and fix what fails. It runs exactly what the self-check will run for your change. {{builder_tests}}
Do not run the whole test suite: the full check runs after you finish, beside the reviews.
If you wrap a command in `timeout`, give it about twice the time stated above; DSH workspace shell commands are killed after at most 10 minutes.
When you are done, stop: the workspace's diff is your answer. The runtime turns it into the next attempt, which the check and the reviews then judge. Return a short completion message.
When you updated an existing test because the brief or a correction changes what it pins, end the message with one line: `Updated tests: <test id> (follows <the ask or correction>), ...`.

## Before you stop
- For each correction made at the design gate and each ask in the brief, find the test that proves it and run it in your workspace.
- Then revert that change in the workspace and run the same test again: it must fail. If it still passes, the test does not prove the change: fix the test, then restore the change and run the test once more.
- A correction counts as met only if a test fails without it. The reviewers check this.
- Avoid a test that calls the helper under test instead of driving the real path the brief names, test inputs nothing uses (such as a verdict list nothing consumes), and assertions on results the test built by hand.

gate_check.gate_prompt: compose one send-back from check failures and review findings without spending an attempt; the combined send-back names every failing test and every review finding of the round; a failing check skips the QA judge and overwatch by graph topology (gate_check → pick_corrections bypasses synthesize_qa → qa_judge → overwatch); at its limit, deliver the attempt as a draft marked check failing; when the check and all reviews passed, proceed

gate_design_review.gate_prompt: reloop to design_doc only for a missing or empty ## Changes; list everything else on the approval card; never fail the run

gate_overwatch.gate_prompt: route on the overwatch's verdict: an unmet correction or a redo for what holds the change back goes to the builder, or, at the review limit, to the report as a draft; a pass to the report; an unreadable verdict is read again once; follow-ups go to the pull request

gate_pitfalls.gate_prompt: reloop once only when there are no parseable pitfalls; otherwise proceed, with what is off listed on the approval card

gate_qa.gate_prompt: route on the QA judge's verdict: a redo for what holds the change back goes to the builder, or, at the review limit, on as a draft; an unreadable verdict is read again once; follow-ups go to the pull request

gate_research.gate_prompt: reloop once only when there is no parseable plan; otherwise proceed, with what is off listed on the approval card

gate_strategy.gate_prompt:
{{design_card}}

Approve the design before the artifact is written? It is in design.md in the run directory. Then, {{delivery}}; delivery.md there says more. Answer proceed to build and deliver it that way, or reloop to have the plan redone.

materialise.notes: commit the emitted files on the run's branch, or write the artifact directory

pick_corrections.gate_prompt: deterministically extract the person's corrections to the approved design from the ledger, after the approval and on every send-back to the builder; skip the agent when none is new

pitfalls_researcher.prompt_template:
Artifact name: {{name}}
Brief: {{brief}}
Repository: {{source}}

## Research scope
{{research_scope}}

## What the research found
{{research}}

## What was wrong with the last attempt
{{pitfalls_review}}

You are the pitfalls researcher. Before any strategy or design exists, identify the risks a correct design must account for. Read the repository and the brief, and produce a risk-ranked list of pitfalls. For a scoped change, list at most five: only the risks a correct design of this change must account for.

For each pitfall, provide:
- **id**: a short identifier in the format PIT-001, PIT-002, etc.
- **risk**: high, medium, or low.
- **category**: exactly one of:
  - `pinning_tests` — tests that pin current behaviour. Name the file, the line, and the exact assertion text. Say whether the change must keep it or deliberately change it.
  - `repo_conventions` — the repository's own rules and conventions, taken from its code, docs and agent instructions (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING, or similar) with citations. Never use a built-in list.
  - `shared_state` — other writers and readers of the files, environment variables, HOME, locks, and processes the change touches.
  - `callers` — callers of the code being changed, and the user paths each serves.
  - `imitated_steps` — the existing step the change imitates, and the settings it reads.
  - `scope_boundaries` — modes and paths that must not change.
- **evidence**: one of these forms:
  - `file:line` — cite a file and line number from the repository (for code that exists).
  - `absent: <path or glob>` — when the pitfall is about something missing (no tests, no config file). A glob like `tests/test_*.py` is accepted. The gate verifies the path or glob does NOT match anything in the worktree.
  - `brief.json` or `research/<slug>.md` — cite a run artifact when evidence comes from the brief or research, not from repository code.
- **prescription**: what a correct design must do about it.

Sort by risk (high first). Write `pitfalls.json` as a JSON array of these objects. Then write `pitfalls.md` as a human-readable rendering of the same list. Do not read strategy.json or design.md — this step is independent of them.

prepare.notes: read the brief and the command that decides whether it is done

prepare_check.gate_prompt: settle the commit the check and the reviews see; every attempt's self-check runs the tests the change touches here (first or fix-up): a failure goes back to emit as a fix-up, spending no attempt and running no review; the full check runs beside the reviews in fork_qa; a limit stop with an applied commit and current check evidence goes to the report as a draft

record_findings.notes: write each direction's finding where the reviews will look for it

research_director.prompt_template:
Artifact name: {{name}}
Brief: {{brief}}
It will be checked by running, from {{check_root}}:
    {{check}}

## Research scope
{{research_scope}}

You are the research director. Decide what has to be learned before this artifact can be designed: between three and five questions for a full design, or one focused question for a scoped change (two or three only when it spans unrelated parts of the code). Each must be answerable by reading {{source}} — including the source code of tools and libraries the change depends on, not only the files it changes — or by running something there. Spawn one subagent per question and have each write its findings to `research/<slug>.md` under the run directory, then write `research-plan.json` yourself.

## Footprint
Record a `footprint` object on every direction, with exactly these three keys, each a list. A direction that touches no code records an empty footprint: `{"existing_functions": [], "new_items": [], "shared_engine": []}`.

- `existing_functions`: each entry is a string `"path:line name"` for an existing function the direction's change modifies: one function per entry, the line its definition starts on, and its path as the target's checkout shows it. Test files, test functions and docs are neither touched functions nor added items.
- `new_items`: each entry is a string naming what is added and the path it goes in — a module, class, graph node, edge, node field, record or data shape, knob, entry point, wiring helper, or any new non-test source file. Give the file:line where it would be added or wired.
- `shared_engine`: a list of `"path:line"` citations of the engine code the change modifies — code that every run of the target passes through, such as its executor, scheduler, worker dispatch, or compilation or lowering step. A function is not an engine because several gates or modes call it. Empty when the change does not touch one.
- Wording in the brief about the change's size ("small", "a one-line fix", "a scoped change", "a full change") is a claim to check against the code, never a footprint.

## What was wrong with the last plan
{{research_review}}

## The plan's shape
Write one JSON array and nothing else, one object per direction:

[{"focus": "<the question this direction answers>",
  "slug": "<a file-name-safe name for it>",
  "finding": "<what the answer is, in one paragraph>",
  "ids": ["FND-<slug>-1", "FND-<slug>-2"]}]

Rules:
- Between three and five directions for a full design, or one to three for a scoped change. The research scope is a fact set by the prepare step.
- `slug` is lower-case letters, digits and dashes only, and `research/<slug>.md` is
  where that direction's long form belongs.
- `finding` states what the answer *is*. A direction nobody could answer says so in
  the finding ("not answered: <why>") rather than being dropped or invented.
- Each finding in `research/<slug>.md` is a heading `### FND-<slug>-<n> — <the finding>`,
  numbered from 1 within the file, and `ids` lists them.
- A plan that says subagents are still working is not a plan: by the time you answer,
  the work is either done or it is not.

route_refine_design.gate_prompt: on a light refine, skip research and strategy and go straight to design_doc

route_strategy.gate_prompt: a scoped change is planned straight from the research; a full design weighs perspectives

synthesize_qa.notes: put this attempt's reviews, its check and its scope in one document, unread; an absent review is not a passed one

check_attempts.description: how many times the emit step may be retried when the artifact does not pass its check

review_attempts.description: how many times the review gates may reloop before stopping; defaults to the same as check_attempts

check_timeout_s.description: how long the brief's check may run

check_attempt_cap.description: hard cap on total check attempts including convergence grants; 0 or a value at or below check_attempts disables the extension

design_review_attempts.description: how many times a design whose ## Changes section is missing or empty is sent back for a rewrite before it goes to the approval gate as it is; every other finding is advisory and never sends it back

name.description: the artifact to design (empty takes the name from the brief)

brief.description: what to build, in the asker's words

check.description: the command that decides whether the artifact works

refusal_attempts.description: consecutive refused emissions before the run stops

judge_rereads.description: how many times a round a judge whose verdict could not be read is asked again, with no builder round, before its gate goes on without it

self_check_fixups.description: how many times the self-check may send an attempt back to emit, spending nothing, before the early stop spends it; a run gets this many times check_attempts

self_check_timeout_s.description: how long the self-check's tests may run before the reviews; never more than a third of check_timeout_s

builder_timeout_s.description: how long the builder's model session may run before timeout; its retry doubles this

refine_design.description: on a refine: light skips research and strategy; full walks the whole design phase

target.description: the git repository to change; empty starts a new project in the projects folder

base.description: the commit, branch or tag the run starts from (default: the target's HEAD, or a new project's main)

worktree.description: work in a worktree of the target on the run's own branch; off writes the artifact under .factory/artifacts instead

setup.description: a command run in the worktree before each check, after its dependencies are installed, such as a build

generate.description: a command run in the worktree after dependencies are installed, before setup and each check; whatever it changes in tracked files is amended into the attempt. A generator that itself needs a build includes that build in its own command

include_uncommitted.description: start from the target's uncommitted changes instead of only committed HEAD; copies modified, staged, untracked and deleted files into the worktree and commits them as the run's base

pr.description: open a pull request once the reviews pass: into the target's default branch, or a new project's own GitHub repository; off keeps the work on the run's local branch, with its pull request text in pull-request.md and finishing commands in delivery.json

repo_owner.description: the GitHub account or organisation a new project's repository is created under (default: the account gh is logged in to)

repo_visibility.description: who can see a new project's GitHub repository

refine.description: an open pull request to follow up, as its URL or owner/repo#number: the run starts from its branch and its result updates it

review_comments.description: with refine: add the pull request's reviews and comments to the run's steering
